abstract: Exoribonuclease-resistant RNAs (xrRNAs) are non-coding RNAs used by viruses to evade host RNase-mediated degradation. In flaviviruses, xrRNAs are thought to share an unusual knot-like fold with the 5'-end threaded through a ring formed by a multi-helix junction and closed by a pseudoknot, but only a handful of high-resolution structures have been solved to date. We combined structure prediction tools with mutational analysis of RNase resistance to determine previously unsolved 3D structures of xrRNAs from the West Nile virus (WNV) and two dengue virus (DENV) serotypes. We first predicted possible pseudoknot structures computationally, then tested them by systematically mutating putatively pseudoknotted bases and assessing RNase resistance to discriminate between models. The successful pseudoknot models were used to predict 3D structures computationally, refining the models by identifying tertiary contacts at the threaded 5' end via another round of mutagenesis and RNase resistance testing. We found that all 3 xrRNAs shared the same threaded knot-like architecture as in experimentally solved flaviviral xrRNAs, with similar tertiary contacts generating an analogous hierarchy of interactions importance for RNase resistance, but the pseudoknot length varied considerably, from 8 pairs in WNV to 2 in DENV2. This work illustrates a powerful new approach for determining xrRNA structures that are hard to obtain by high-resolution experimental methods by integrating computational predictions with functional assays.
